implementation_notes: The C# compiler turns `lock (x) { ... }` into Monitor.Enter inside a try with Monitor.Exit in the matching finally, so the mutual-exclusion lock is released on exceptions and early returns - the pattern is language syntax, and the classic guard class is unnecessary. The monitor is reentrant for the owning thread. Use a dedicated private reference object as the lock target, and remember that `await` is not allowed inside a lock body, so asynchronous critical sections need SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync or an async-aware lock instead.
pitfalls: Locking on `this`, a Type, a string literal or another shared/interned object lets unrelated code lock the same monitor and deadlock or starve you; always use a dedicated private object.
Monitors are reentrant and callbacks inside the lock can re-enter your API without blocking, hiding re-entrancy bugs until the object state is already inconsistent.
`await` is a compile error inside lock, but Task.Wait()/Result are legal and can deadlock the thread pool - keep the body synchronous and short.
Lock ordering is not enforced; two locks taken in different orders still deadlock.

variants.name: System.Threading.Lock with the lock statement (C# 13 / .NET 9)
variants.implementation_notes: Starting with C# 13 and .NET 9 the recommended lock target is System.Threading.Lock: when the compiler knows the expression is a Lock it emits `using (x.EnterScope())` and a ref-struct scope instead of Monitor, which is measurably cheaper. The scope-bound guarantee is unchanged - the generated using statement disposes the scope on every path. Existing reference-type lock statements keep working unchanged, so the migration is a type change on the lock field, not a restructure of the critical sections.
pitfalls: EnterScope() returns a ref struct: it cannot be boxed, stored in a field or captured by a lambda, so keep it in the using statement.
Lock has no Wait/Pulse: condition-variable style coordination still needs Monitor, SemaphoreSlim or a Channel.
Mixing Lock and Monitor on the same object is a bug - the two mechanisms do not exclude each other, so one thread can hold Lock while another enters the Monitor.
Lock is reentrant, so nested acquisition silently succeeds and hides design problems.
